strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: predicting human response times under changing environmental cues. Combining learned task representations, evidence accumulation, and reinforcement learning is a well-motivated direction.

The behavioral dataset is valuable: 21,157 responses across two days and four feedback conditions, with 36 participants retained after exclusions. Random and adaptive feedback provide useful variation beyond a simple pressure/no-pressure comparison.

Evaluation includes individual, group, pooled, and leave-one-participant-out settings. The hybrid model achieves lower reported aggregate MAPE than Pure DRL in all four settings, and learned task features outperform raw-number representations.
The manuscript provides public data, model, and code links, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic interpretation is insufficiently supported. The Methods substitute an assumed sigmoid trajectory, determined by SVM outputs, for diffusion dynamics without validating its correspondence to human evidence accumulation. Matching terminal response times does not establish that the learned per-frame adjustments represent cognitive mechanisms. Figure 7 also shows nonzero 'time pressure' effects in the no-pressure group, indicating that these adjustments can absorb baseline prediction error.

The comparison does not isolate the proposed contribution. Pure DRL uses whole-video Inception features, whereas the hybrid uses a frame-level CNN; action scales and episode structures also differ. Consequently, the accuracy and training-time improvements cannot confidently be attributed to the accumulation model. Matched supervised response-time predictors, conventional or time-varying DDM baselines, and stimulus-removal or frame-order ablations would substantially strengthen the evidence.

The predictive improvements are modest and lack uncertainty estimates. Figure 6(e) reports MAPE decreasing from 0.3034 to 0.2999 in pooled evaluation and from 0.3037 to 0.2905 in leave-one-participant-out evaluation. Participant-level confidence intervals and repeated-seed results are needed to establish the reliability of these gains.

Important training details remain unclear. The manuscript does not clearly identify which no-pressure observations train the SVM baseline or whether that baseline is refitted within every held-out-participant fold. These details matter for auditing generalization and interpreting corrections as pressure effects. The sigmoid parameterization, perturbation coefficient λ, and numerical adaptive-feedback thresholds are also unspecified.

The human-study inference needs clarification. Between-group post hoc tests are described as paired despite independently assigned, unequal-sized groups. Criteria for excluding three participants as 'extreme outliers' are not provided. With only 7–10 retained participants per condition and a reported group response-time effect of p = 0.044, corrected analyses and exclusion-sensitivity checks are important.

The evidence supports a promising response-time predictor on one arithmetic task more clearly than an explanatory model of dynamic stress and logical reasoning. The broader claims about cognitive mechanisms and transfer to other tasks or stimulus modalities remain untested. Together with the comparison and validation gaps, this makes weak rejection appropriate despite the useful dataset and preliminary gains.
